---
id: c-line-reverser
title: Reverse a File of Unknown Size
difficulty: Medium
order: 1
tags: malloc, realloc, dynamic arrays, strings
time_limit: 2
---
## Statement
Read **all** lines from standard input and print them in **reverse order**, with the characters of each line also reversed.

You don't know how many lines there are (up to 200 000) or how long each one is (a single line can be 1 000 000 characters). Fixed-size buffers like `char line[1000]` won't work. Build:

- a growable string for reading one line of any length (`getchar` until `'\n'` or `EOF`), and
- a growable array of `char *` holding every line,

both grown with `realloc` **geometrically** (doubling). Free everything before exiting.

The last line may or may not end with `'\n'`. Treat both the same, and don't produce an extra empty line for a trailing newline. Empty lines in the middle are real lines and must be kept.

## Starter
```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

/* Reads one line (without the '\n') into a malloc'd string and stores its length in *len.
   Returns NULL at end of input. Caller frees. */
char *read_line(size_t *len) {
    return NULL;
}

int main(void) {
    /* TODO: read every line into a growable array, then print in reverse, each line reversed */
    return 0;
}
```

## Hints
- Line buffer: start with `cap = 16`. When `len + 1 == cap`, double `cap` and `realloc`. Always leave room for `'\0'`.
- Lines array: the same doubling pattern with `char **lines`.
- Return NULL from `read_line` only when you hit `EOF` **before reading any character**. A final line without `'\n'` is still a line.
- Reverse in place with two indices. Then print with `fputs` + `putchar('\n')`, or `fwrite`. Avoid `printf("%s")` per character.

## Solution
```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

char *read_line(size_t *len) {
    size_t cap = 16, n = 0;
    char *s = malloc(cap);
    if (!s) return NULL;
    int c;
    while ((c = getchar()) != EOF && c != '\n') {
        if (n + 1 == cap) {
            char *tmp = realloc(s, cap * 2);
            if (!tmp) { free(s); return NULL; }
            s = tmp;
            cap *= 2;
        }
        s[n++] = (char)c;
    }
    if (c == EOF && n == 0) { free(s); return NULL; }   /* nothing left */
    s[n] = '\0';
    *len = n;
    return s;
}

static void reverse(char *s, size_t n) {
    for (size_t i = 0, j = n; i + 1 < j; i++, j--) {
        char t = s[i]; s[i] = s[j - 1]; s[j - 1] = t;
    }
}

int main(void) {
    size_t cap = 16, count = 0;
    char **lines = malloc(cap * sizeof *lines);
    size_t *lens = malloc(cap * sizeof *lens);
    if (!lines || !lens) return 1;

    char *s;
    size_t len;
    while ((s = read_line(&len)) != NULL) {
        if (count == cap) {
            cap *= 2;
            char **t1 = realloc(lines, cap * sizeof *lines);
            size_t *t2 = realloc(lens, cap * sizeof *lens);
            if (!t1 || !t2) return 1;
            lines = t1;
            lens = t2;
        }
        lines[count] = s;
        lens[count] = len;
        count++;
    }
    for (size_t i = count; i-- > 0;) {
        reverse(lines[i], lens[i]);
        fwrite(lines[i], 1, lens[i], stdout);
        putchar('\n');
        free(lines[i]);
    }
    free(lines);
    free(lens);
    return 0;
}
```

Two geometric growth loops make the whole program **O(total input)**: each byte is copied O(1) times on average across all reallocations. The `realloc` result goes into a temporary so a failure doesn't leak. `read_line` distinguishes "end of input" (EOF before any character) from "last line without newline" (EOF after some characters), which is a classic off-by-one-line bug. The loop `for (i = count; i-- > 0;)` is the idiomatic way to count down with an unsigned index without underflow.
